summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the surviving sodomy-law articles resolved that the current criminal code contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct; those articles reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no equivalent provision for heterosexual acts, and Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy.

Enforcement against same-sex couples has historically run through public-order offences rather than a sodomy statute. A former law criminalising acts that violated "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for displays of affection, and a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code repealed it. Police closed several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo in 2006 as part of a harassment programme. In 2012 officers broke up the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride parade and arrested marchers on the ground that they were improperly using the national flag. Reports indicate that visible, politically active LGBTQ groups are frequent targets of government crackdowns, sometimes with the support of religious leaders.

There is no legal gender recognition. A trans visitor has no route to a chosen name or gender marker on Dominican documents, and the authorities recognise no domestic process for it. The sole concession on record is a June 2018 executive decree issued by President Danilo Medina that gave 35 transgender Dominicans, among them television journalist Mía Cepeda, the possibility of changing their legal name to match their gender identity; it did not provide for a change of gender marker. A 2017 ILGA poll found that only a plurality of 5% of Dominicans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

No general anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. Discrimination on those grounds is not illegal in employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services, public accommodations or health care, and many LGBTQ people consequently remain in the closet. Since 2011, Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, but the protection runs only within that field. The Dominican Republic has accepted UPR recommendations on the rights of intersex persons and on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, an international-commitment record for which the sources show no domestic implementation detail.

Family law recognises no legal status between persons of the same sex, neither marriage nor civil or domestic partnership, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. The 2010 constitutional amendment added Article 55, under which the State shall promote and protect family organisation based on marriage between a man and a woman, so same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned. Article 41 of Law 544-14 on Private International Law could justify recognition, since a marriage is valid if considered such by the law of the place of celebration, the national law or the domicile of at least one spouse. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion on 9 January 2018 holding that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage, and several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it.

Citizens have a constitutional right to access health care services, but health care programmes for the LGBTQ community have generally focused on HIV/AIDS education, often run by non-governmental organisations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos.
tangentialFactors:
The social climate is shaped by the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations, whose mores hold significant sway over public policy and prevailing attitudes. Because most residents hold conservative views, the major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals, a figure recorded before the Constitutional Court's 2024 review.

Organised domestic opposition has previously been directed at visible foreign representatives. The tenure of openly gay US Ambassador James "Wally" Brewster from 2013 to 2017 drew regular insults from religious leaders and some politicians, an unsuccessful evangelical petition demanding his expulsion, and attacks on LGBT Dominicans reported in April 2016. He spoke at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 July 2016, and his departure in 2017 left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence, exposing a polarised climate.

Civic engagement exists alongside that hostility. More than 300 activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT and intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo in April 2017 at which Dominican government officials spoke. Nairovi Castillo, executive director of COTRAVETD, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers co-founded in 2004, has given a first-hand account of trans struggles in the country.
localsOnly:
Residents share the visitor's legal position on criminalisation and relationship recognition: same-sex relations are not an offence, and no marriage or partnership status is available to same-sex couples. Household formation carries no derived rights for same-sex partners.

A name change matching gender identity was made possible for a defined group of 35 transgender Dominicans under the June 2018 executive decree, with television journalist Mía Cepeda among those who subsequently changed her name. The sources do not describe a general application route beyond that group.

Discrimination in employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services, public accommodations and health care is lawful except where it arises under the HIV/AIDS framework of Law 135/2011. Health services addressing LGBTQ needs are largely delivered by non-governmental organisations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos, with an emphasis on HIV/AIDS education rather than trans-specific care.

The government has accepted international recommendations on intersex persons' rights and on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity through the Universal Periodic Review process. Community organisations including COTRAVETD have operated since 2004, and the country has hosted regional LGBT and intersex conferences attended by Dominican officials.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the June 2018 executive decree on legal names remains open to applicants beyond the 35 individuals it named is unresolved; the sources record the decree and its beneficiaries but no standing procedure or eligibility criteria.

No enforcement record for Law 135/2011 appears in the inventory. Whether the anti-discrimination provisions have been invoked, by whom, and with what outcome is not sourced.

The application of Article 41 of Law 544-14 to a specific same-sex marriage is not documented here, and no case in which Dominican authorities recognised a foreign same-sex marriage is recorded. Implementation of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 is asserted by several Dominican legal experts as obligatory but is not shown as having occurred.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence incidents with dates and outcomes. Reports of crackdowns on visible LGBTQ activism are cited in general terms, with the 2006 venue closures and the 2012 Pride arrests as the only dated episodes. Public-opinion figures come from a single 2017 poll and predate the 2024 constitutional ruling.
